samples.text:
Tourism is a very big industry and many cities and islands are visited by millions of people every year. Some people think that famous tourist places should limit the number of tourists to protect the local people. I agree with this idea.

First of all, too many tourists cause a lot of problems for the local communities. The streets become very crowded, and local people cannot live their normal life. For example, in some famous old cities, residents cannot even walk to work or go shopping easily because there are tourists everywhere. Also, the prices of food and houses become very high, because many owners prefer to rent their apartments to tourists for more money. As a result, local families have to move away from the place where they grew up.

Secondly, a large number of tourist can damage the environment. They produce a lot of rubbish and use a lot of water and energy. Beautiful beaches and historical buildings can be destroyed if too many people visit them every day. If this happen, the place will not be attractive anymore, and in the future tourists will stop coming.

On the other hand, some people say that tourism bring money and jobs to the local people. This is true, but if the number is limited, the tourists can still come and spend money. The place can also increase the price of tickets so that it still earn enough money.

In conclusion, I agree that popular tourist destinations should limit the number of visitors every year. It will protect the local communities and the environment, and it will also help these places to stay beautiful for the future.

samples.text:
In recent years, several popular destinations have struggled with overcrowding, and some people believe that annual limits on visitor numbers are needed to protect local communities. I agree with this view to a large extent, although I think such limits should be applied flexibly and combined with other measures.

The main argument for limiting visitors is the impact of mass tourism on residents' daily lives. In many historic cities and small islands, streets, public transport and beaches become so crowded during peak season that locals can no longer use them normally. In addition, the growth of short-term holiday rentals has pushed up housing costs, forcing many families and young people to leave the neighbourhoods where they have always lived. Without controls, some destinations risk becoming places that exist only for tourists.

Excessive tourism also damages the natural and cultural assets that attract visitors in the first place. Fragile environments, such as coral reefs and mountain trails, can suffer long-term harm from heavy use, while ancient sites deteriorate when thousands of people walk through them each day. Setting a maximum number of visitors can help preserve these places for future generations.

Nonetheless, tourism is a vital source of income for many communities, and a strict cap could lead to job losses in hotels, restaurants and shops. For this reason, limits should be carefully planned. Destinations could introduce daily quotas for the most vulnerable sites, charge higher fees during the busiest months, and encourage visitors to travel in the off-season or visit less well-known areas nearby. By this way, the economic benefit is spread more evenly.

In conclusion, I believe popular destinations are justified in limiting visitor numbers to protect local residents and the environment. However, these limits should be part of a wider strategy which balances the needs of communities with the economic advantages of tourism.

samples.text:
Few issues illustrate the tension between economic opportunity and quality of life as sharply as mass tourism. Some argue that the most popular destinations should cap the number of visitors each year to protect local communities. I agree with this principle, but I believe that rigid annual limits are often less effective than more targeted forms of visitor management.

There is little doubt that unchecked tourism can seriously undermine residents' wellbeing. In some historic cities, the conversion of apartments into holiday lets has driven up rents to the point where long-standing residents are priced out, while local shops give way to souvenir outlets. Overcrowded streets, congested public transport and constant noise can make everyday life exhausting. When a community begins to feel like a stage set for visitors, the very authenticity that attracted tourists is lost.

The environmental case is equally compelling. Coastal ecosystems, mountain paths and archaeological sites can absorb only so much footfall before suffering lasting damage. For such places, limiting access is not merely desirable but essential if they are to survive in any recognisable form.

However, a single annual quota is a rather crude tool. Tourist pressure is usually concentrated in particular seasons, days and districts, so a yearly cap may do little to relieve overcrowding at peak times while needlessly turning visitors away in quieter periods. It could also harm the many residents whose livelihoods depend on tourism. More refined measures, such as timed entry to key sites, daily limits on cruise-ship arrivals, restrictions on short-term rentals and higher fees in peak season, can address the specific sources of pressure while preserving the income that tourism brings.

In conclusion, popular destinations are right to control visitor numbers in order to protect their residents and environment. Yet this is best achieved through flexible, carefully targeted management rather than a blunt annual ceiling.
samples.why: Well-developed, nuanced position · ideas logically sequenced and fully supported · effective, precise cohesion · wide, natural vocabulary and collocation · complex structures used accurately and flexibly.
